entityDossier.whatItIs: A claimed saucer-shaped craft, called the Alien Reproduction Vehicle and the Flux Liner, said to have been shown in a hangar at Norton Air Force Base on 12 November 1988. No record of its existence has been opened. The whole account descends from one second-hand relay: an industrial designer said he saw three such craft, and an aerospace illustrator who was not present drew them from that verbal description. Two primary documents carry the description, William B. Scott's unpublished 1990 interview notes and the Disclosure Project's April 2001 Briefing Document, and they are why this node exists, not evidence that the craft does.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: It is on this map as the worked example of a rule the board adopted on 18 September 2026: the thing claimed about is a node in its own right, and it is the hub every claimant runs into. Ten people arguing about a place, joined only to each other, hide the convergence; joined to the place, they show it. This is the first craft node the board has ever carried, and its edges are deliberately mixed: the sole eyewitness, the illustrator who drew it, the trade-press editor who investigated and never published, the anonymous site that sells reconstructions of it, and a government scientist who says it never existed. Its degree means a lot is claimed here. It does not mean any of it is true, and the tier on each edge says which is which.
entityDossier.narrative: The argument for a node with no evidence behind it is that the alternative is worse. Before this build the board carried Steven Greer, the Disclosure Project, the Brown patents and the contractor estate, and carried nothing for the object all of them are talking about. A reader could not see that the ARV is a single claim with many carriers, because the carriers were joined to each other and to institutions, never to the thing itself. Building the hub makes the shape legible and, more usefully, makes the shape falsifiable: every edge into it is dated, typed and tiered, so the reader can count how much of the convergence is documented. The answer here is: very little. The strongest artefact is a working file an Aviation Week editor never published, and inside it the witness refuses to stand behind his own figures and disowns part of the drawing made from his account. The sizes then grow more precise with each retelling, which is the opposite of what happens to a measurement. The claimed lift mechanism is attributed to a Thomas Townsend Brown patent, and the board's own record is that neither Brown patent claims anti-gravity: both claim thrust by electrical fields in a dielectric medium. That join is the reason this thread belongs to a board about defense contractors at all, and it is also the reason it does not support what it is usually cited to support.

claims.text: THE SIZES HAVE DRIFTED, AND THE DRIFT RUNS ONE WAY, across three opened documents. The 1990 interview notes give 'The small one was like 20 ft, the next 60 ft. diameter and the next one,...maybe 120 ft. diam. Just a guess; don't hold me to that.' The April 2001 Briefing Document gives the smallest as 'about 24 feet in diameter at its widest part, right at the base', the next as '60 feet in diameter at the base', and 'the largest of these vehicles was about 120 to 130 feet in diameter'. The arvp.co.uk FLUX 1988 page, read 18 September 2026, gives 'one with a 130-foot diameter, another with a 60-foot diameter, and a smaller one measuring 24 feet in diameter', with no disclaimer. Each retelling is more precise than the last about a figure the witness explicitly refused to stand behind.
claims.source: Scott interview notes transcript p 10, https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , 1990-12-03; Disclosure Project Briefing Document section 3.8.5, https://archive.org/stream/DisclosureProjectBriefingDocument/DisclosureProjectBriefingDocument_djvu.txt , 2000-12; arvp.co.uk FLUX 1988 page, https://www.arvp.co.uk/flux-01/ , read 2026-09-18

claims.text: THE WITNESS DISOWNS PART OF THE DRAWING. Shown McCandlish's sketches in December 1990, Sorensen says of the manned vehicle: 'this is probably the farthest from what I saw, and no, I didn't see anything with an intake up above the windows like this', and 'mark extrapolates a bit too much'. Of the saucer drawing he says the opposite: 'you've got a drawing, as accurate as I could get [the round, saucer-looking thing]. This dwg is so GD..accurate that I can't be much more specific than this.'
claims.source: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 10, 1990-12-03

claims.text: The April 2001 Briefing Document is the origin in print of the craft's two names, in the illustrator's own words: 'Well, this craft was what they called the Alien Reproduction Vehicle; it was also nicknamed the Flux Liner.'

The 1990 primary document gives the three craft their nursery-rhyme names and the witness's own guessed sizes: 'This was a really interesting craft--there were three of them. When I walked into the room....well, I thought of something stupid--like a nursery rhyme: daddy bear, mommy bear, baby bear. Like they'd been put in a Xerox machine--the same proportions, just diff. sizes. The small one was like 20 ft, the next 60 ft. diameter and the next one,...maybe 120 ft. diam. Just a guess; don't hold me to that.'
claims.source: William B. Scott, interview notes on 'Brad', https://www.arvp.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/SORENSEN-1990-INTERVIEW.pdf , transcript p 10, 1990-12-03

openQuestions: The Aviation Week and Space Technology issue of 1 October 1990, which the 1990 notes name as carrying McCandlish's two paintings. It is the only element of this thread published in the contemporary trade press and nobody has opened it.
The McCandlish cut-away drawing itself, as printed in the Disclosure Project Briefing Document's plate section, which this session did not extract.
Whether any record of Brad Sorensen exists under that surname. The 1990 document gives a first name, a school, a client list and an hourly rate, and nobody in the opened record appears to have tried.

entityDossier.whatItIs: One of the United States' prime defense contractors, builder of the B-2 and the B-21 Raider at Air Force Plant 42, and, from 2006 to 2017, the leader of National Security Technologies LLC, the consortium that held the management and operating contract for the Nevada Test Site after Bechtel Nevada.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: It sits at the intersection of the two things this board tracks: work at the deepest classification levels, and custody of the Nevada complex. The stealth bomber programmes put it inside compartmented aircraft development at Plant 42; the NSTec contract put it in operational control of the ground the retrieval and reverse-engineering claims are attached to. Senate Appropriations investigator Richard D'Amato is reported to have named it, with Lockheed Martin and EG&G, as the kind of private entity inside which a cover-up could feasibly sit. That last is a Tier 3 report and is carried as one.
entityDossier.narrative: Northrop Grumman crossed this map's floor on the build of 18 September 2026, which is ordinary churn and not a finding: the board's practice, recorded in data/l0-shorts.json, is that a corpus build pushing a node over the L0 floor gets its dossier authored. What is worth stating is that its case for the map does not rest on the edge that moved it. That edge is a Tier 2 self-stated client list, an illustrator saying he did conceptual work for the company, with no personnel record and no contract record opened, and it proves nothing about the company at all. The case rests instead on two Tier 1 claims already on its record: the DOE listing that makes it the Nevada Test Site's management and operating contractor for eleven years, and USAspending's record of prime contract obligations in the tens of billions since FY2008. A board about who holds the programme's money and the programme's ground has to carry the company that held both. The D'Amato report is the weakest thing here and the most quoted, and it is graded Tier 3 for that reason.

claims.text: National Security Technologies LLC, a Northrop Grumman-led consortium, succeeded Bechtel Nevada as management and operating contractor for the Nevada Test Site from 2006.
claims.source: DOE/OSTI records listing Bechtel Nevada and National Security Technologies, LLC as successive Nevada Test Site research organisations

claims.text: USAspending records prime contract obligations to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation in the tens of billions of dollars since FY2008.

Senate Appropriations investigator Richard D'Amato is reported to have considered it 'entirely feasible' that the cover-up sat inside a private company such as Lockheed Martin, EG&G or Northrop Grumman. Reasoning: reported at second hand by George Knapp; D'Amato's own public statement says the inquiry found nothing meriting further investigation.
claims.source: George Knapp via Liberation Times, 28 February 2023

openQuestions: Whether any NSTec contract document names the scope of the management and operating role at the Nevada Test Site beyond the DOE research-organization listing.
What the USAspending prime contract obligations break down to by programme, which the recipient search does not itself show.
